summary.text: Take the counterexample \(n=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\), where \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime, and rewrite \(a(n)=2\sigma(n)-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\). Multiplicativity gives \(\sigma(n)=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010\) and \(\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011\), whose difference is \(1\), although \(n\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e\) denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(m\). The deficiency used in the definition of A296075 is
\[
\delta(m)=2m-\sigma(m),
\]
so the sequence is the integer-valued function
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) at which this sum is \(1\).

Take
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009.
\]
The two odd factors are prime. For completeness, this can be established by the following short primality certificates. We use the elementary order criterion: if, for an integer \(m>1\), the complete factorization of \(m-1\) is known and there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{m-1}\equiv 1\pmod m
\]
and
\[
b^{(m-1)/r}\not\equiv1\pmod m
\]
for every prime divisor \(r\) of \(m-1\), then \(m\) is prime. Indeed, these conditions say that the multiplicative order of \(b\) modulo \(m\) is exactly \(m-1\). This order divides \(\varphi(m)\), while \(\varphi(m)\le m-1\), so \(\varphi(m)=m-1\), which is possible only when \(m\) is prime.

The following factorizations and modular residues are obtained by ordinary repeated squaring. In every row, the chosen base raised to the full exponent \(m-1\) has residue \(1\); the displayed list gives, for each distinct prime \(r\mid m-1\), the residue of the base raised to \((m-1)/r\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
m&m-1&b&\bigl(r,\ b^{(m-1)/r}\bmod m\bigr)\\ \hline
5&2^2&2&(2,4)\\
7&2\cdot3&3&(2,6),(3,2)\\
19&2\cdot3^2&2&(2,18),(3,7)\\
29&2^2\cdot7&2&(2,28),(7,16)\\
229&2^2\cdot3\cdot19&6&(2,228),(3,134),(19,165)\\
57251&2\cdot5^3\cdot229&2&(2,57250),(5,55371),(229,48088)\\
4409&2^3\cdot19\cdot29&3&(2,4408),(19,209),(29,3965)\\
458009&2^3\cdot57251&3&(2,458008),(57251,6561).
\end{array}
\]
None of the listed residues is \(1\). Starting with the evident primality of \(2\) and \(3\), the rows successively prove that \(5,7,19,29,229,57251,4409\), and \(458009\) are prime (the ordering of the rows may be read according to their dependencies: \(229\) uses \(19\), \(57251\) uses \(5\) and \(229\), \(4409\) uses \(19\) and \(29\), and \(458009\) uses \(57251\)). Thus the displayed expression for \(N\) is a product of powers of three distinct primes.

We now reduce the defining sum for \(a(n)\). Splitting the two terms gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=2\sum_{d\mid n}d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-T(n),
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
T(n):=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Both \(\sigma\) and \(T\) are multiplicative. To recall why, if \(x\) and \(y\) are coprime, every divisor of \(xy\) has a unique expression \(uv\), where \(u\mid x\) and \(v\mid y\), and \(u,v\) are coprime. Consequently
\[
\sigma(xy)=\sum_{u\mid x}\sum_{v\mid y}uv
          =\sigma(x)\sigma(y).
\]
Using this identity in the same unique divisor decomposition gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(xy)
 &=\sum_{u\mid x}\sum_{v\mid y}\sigma(uv)\\
 &=\sum_{u\mid x}\sum_{v\mid y}\sigma(u)\sigma(v)
 =T(x)T(y).
\end{aligned}
\]

For a prime power \(p^e\), these functions have the direct forms
\[
\sigma(p^e)=1+p+\cdots+p^e
\]
and
\[
T(p^e)=\sum_{i=0}^e\sigma(p^i)
      =\sum_{i=0}^e\sum_{j=0}^i p^j.
\]
We evaluate these expressions for the three prime-power factors of \(N\).

For \(2^{14}\),
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767.
\]
Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{i=0}^{14}(1+2+\cdots+2^i)\\
 &=\sum_{i=0}^{14}(2^{i+1}-1)\\
 &=(2+2^2+\cdots+2^{15})-15\\
 &=(2^{16}-2)-15=65519.
\end{aligned}
\]
For a prime \(p\) occurring to the first power,
\[
\sigma(p)=p+1,
\qquad
T(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &\sigma&T\\ \hline
4409&4410&4411\\
458009&458010&458011.
\end{array}
\]

Because the three prime-power factors of \(N\) are pairwise coprime, multiplicativity now gives
\[
\sigma(N)=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010
         =66{,}183{,}576{,}284{,}700
\]
and
\[
T(N)=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011
    =132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\sigma(N)-T(N)\\
 &=2(66{,}183{,}576{,}284{,}700)
   -132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399\\
 &=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}400
   -132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally,
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009
 =33{,}085{,}221{,}781{,}504,
\]
so in particular \(N\ne1\) and \(N\ne12\). Thus \(a(N)=1\) for a positive integer \(N\) outside the proposed pair \(\{1,12\}\). This single counterexample disproves the assertion that, for every positive integer \(n\), one has \(a(n)=1\) if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n=12\).
